column_numbering: Negative numbers counted back from the end of the roll: cols. -16 to -1, where col. -1 is the last column of the roll. The authors chose negative numbering because they expect earlier (preceding) columns to be found later. Col. -16 is the first (leftmost) column revealed.
typical_lines_per_column: Prose: segmentation has revealed up to 18 consecutive lines per column so far. The edition prints 18 lines in most columns (cols. -11, -10, -8, -7, -5, -4, -3, -2), 19 in cols. -9 and -6, and 12-13 in cols. -16 to -12. The prose estimates the unrevealed lower 5.38 cm could hold a further 8/9 lines if it has no lower margin. Simple addition gives about 26-27 lines per column, but the paper never states a total.
intercolumn_cm: about 1.7 (stated as blank spaces of about 17 mm); average column-to-column distance 7.9 (79 mm)
any_statement_on_title_position: The authors say the end title is probably hidden near the revealed final columns, in an area not yet segmented. It has not been found yet. The Vesuvius Challenge launched a first Title Prize for this roll on 5 June 2024, and the authors expected submissions in the coming months.
hand_or_scribe_layout_notes: Script datable between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD. Layout of the text described as regular and organic. The scribe uses punctuation marks (paragraphos, diple) and an asteriskos as a filler at the end of a line (fig. 2). In the edition, paragraphos and diple signs appear in the left margin in several columns (e.g. cols. -15, -14, -7, -6), and a line-end asteriskos appears in col. -12, l. 7. At least one scribal correction: at col. -4, l. 3 a wrong letter is replaced by the correct one written above the line. The edition's sigla also mark a letter added above the line at col. -9, l. 5. Fn. 9 notes a possible similar case at col. -3, l. 13 f. The apparatus notes a possible blank space (vacat) inside col. -9, l. 7.
roll_physical_notes: Unopened carbonized roll, virtually unwrapped. The revealed strip is about 1.2 m long and covers the last 16 columns. Col. -16 shows only a few final letters of 7 lines, plus traces at the line-ends of ll. 8-12 in the edition. Cols. -15 to -1 are complete in width. Height: the revealed portion reaches a maximum of 11.37 cm; the whole roll is 16.75 cm tall, so 5.38 cm in the lower portion are still unrevealed. The upper margin is lost: segmentation has reached the upper edge of the papyrus. The virtually unwrapped portion has a clearly wavy outline, which the authors put down to material damage; the roll is taller on one side than the other. Fn. 6 says the wavy outline in the earlier First Letters Prize images, made before segmentation reached the upper edge, came from digital damage. All measurements come from scan data of the crumpled, shrunken roll, so original sizes, especially height, may be slightly larger. The authors say the roll has approximately 160 columns in total, and about two-thirds of 15 columns can be read. Between cols. -12 and -11, from l. 13 onward (especially left of l. 17), the Grand Prize images show apparent traces in the intercolumn. These are not in the transcription. The authors think they could be a scribal correction or other paratextual element, AI noise, or part of a previous winding picked up by segmentation (a 'virtual sottoposto'). At col. -14, l. 6 a small grey rectangle in the first images was judged to be a segmentation flaw rather than a hole.
scans_used: Scan data acquired in 2019 (EduceLab, University of Kentucky); micro-CT. The paper gives no scan resolution.
extraction_notes: Pages cited are the journal page numbers (the article runs pp. 9-27). In the PDF, PDF page = journal page minus 2; the PDF also has front matter and a blank final page. (1) last_column_is_short = true is inferred from the edition, not stated in prose. In the edition, every column from -16 to -2 ends with a lacuna sign, but col. -1 ends after its last line with no lacuna sign and with a final stop. Col. -1 does begin with a lacuna sign, like all columns. (2) last_column_n_lines_preserved = 7 comes from the line numbering: the introduction cites the last line as col. -1, l. 7, and the edition puts the line number 5 against the 4th printed line. But the edition prints only 6 text lines for col. -1, so l. 1 is not printed. The apparatus has one note keyed 'before l. 1'. This is an internal ambiguity: it is either 6 printed lines numbered 2-7, or a typesetting offset. (3) No original line count is given for col. -1. (4) Lower margin: its presence is unknown. The 8/9-line estimate explicitly assumes the unrevealed lower 5.38 cm has no lower margin. (5) No number of lines lost at the top is given. The paper says only that the upper margin is lost, and every column begins with a lacuna sign in the edition. (6) Written column height, line spacing and letter height are not stated. The 11.37 cm figure is the maximum height of the revealed strip, not a column height. (7) No coronis, end sign, blank space after the last column, stichometric sign or column-count mark is mentioned anywhere. (8) Numbering offset: line numbers in the earlier First Letters Prize images are one lower than in this edition (e.g. col. -15, l. 5 = l. 4 in the earlier image; col. -14, l. 6 = l. 5; col. -15, l. 4 = l. 3). (9) Discrepancy: the prose says up to 18 lines per column, but the edition numbers 19 lines in cols. -9 and -6. (10) At col. -15, l. 4, an oblique tick seen in the earlier images is absent from the Grand Prize images. The authors say there was no space for a punctuation mark there.
